body.text: On November 10, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will be in Manila for the ASEAN summit. The hope is that he’ll be able to announce Canada’s first free trade agreement with the bloc, a deal that, according to International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, is more than 90 percent complete. This would be a very positive outcome for the current government’s push for greater trade diversification.
However, partners in Southeast Asia may have questions on the limits of Canada’s engagement with Beijing. Those doubts will linger as long as Ottawa does not make them clear.

In January, Carney met Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Beijing, where they hashed out an agreement to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, with Canada reducing tariffs on 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles. In May, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited Ottawa and announced that it would be possible for Canada to double its exports to China. Days prior to this meeting, HMCS Charlottetown conducted a freedom of navigation transit through the Taiwan Strait, in defiance of Chinese warnings.

On their own, each of these acts served to promote Canada’s national interest. However, these actions did not occur in a vacuum, and the lack of an explanation that situates both policies as a broader part of Canadian foreign policy makes them appear incoherent. Carney’s government has hit the right notes on foreign policy, and is seeking to foster positive engagement with long-term partners. However, if Canada is to further cultivate its relationships in the Indo-Pacific, it needs a clearer articulation of its regional ambitions and its political limits.

In its 2022 Indo-Pacific Strategy, Ottawa described engagement with a region of 40 economies, 4 billion people, and $47.19 trillion in economic activity as a crucial step in the country’s future growth. Already, the Indo-Pacific is home to six of Canada’s top 13 trading partners, and Ottawa’s engagement efforts in the region are only growing. In 2023, ASEAN and Canada deepened cooperation through a Strategic Partnership. In March, Carney’s tour of the region saw him produce a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership with Japan, and intensified cooperation on defense and critical minerals with Australia, as well as a future promise to work out an economic partnership agreement with India. Moreover, the Royal Canadian Navy deploys three warships in the region every year under Operation HORIZON.

The basis for future Indo-Pacific engagement is set. However, Canada will not benefit from doing everything at once. As the region rapidly develops and dynamic inter-state issues continue to manifest, Ottawa must be prepared to clearly identify and signal its priorities.

The clearest point of contention is in Canada’s relationship with China. Ottawa’s engagement with Beijing should not be based on counter-balancing Washington if its net effect is that it causes discomfort in the capitals of the Philippines, Vietnam, and Indonesia. Canada clearly identifies these states as partners in the Indo-Pacific Strategy; they also deal with the brunt of China’s coercive attempts at enforcing its maritime claims in the South China Sea Without clearly defining the limitations of Ottawa’s engagement with Beijing, and further articulating the support that it is willing to provide partners, Carney’s government risks undercutting the regional position it has successfully cultivated.

Similarly, the Royal Canadian Navy’s participation in this year’s edition of the Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) naval exercise, which brought together 30 nations and over 30,000 personnel, was a strong signal that Canada is committed to working with allies to ensure interoperability and readiness while maintaining peace in the Pacific. Building on this effort, Ottawa should seek to leverage its new appetite for defense procurement reform with a strategic shift toward supporting its partners in Asia.

Canada’s current largest overseas deployment is located in Latvia, where it commands a NATO brigade of roughly 3,000 soldiers from 14 allied countries. This deployment has been extended until 2029, and Canada has invested more than $315 million in infrastructure there. This is an important display of Canada’s willingness to contribute combat power in defense of its allies. However, in Europe, Canada is just one nation among many doing its part. In Asia, the contribution of a single frigate, a detachment of aircraft, or even a training battalion would have a disproportionate effect on demonstrating Canada’s willingness to ensure regional security, and fostering cooperation.

Moreover, many ASEAN partners are wary of welcoming deeper military cooperation with Washington, as they fear the effect it may have on their sovereignty and on their relations with Beijing. By acknowledging these sensitivities, Ottawa can reassure partners, and position itself as an alternative partner with far less baggage.

In support of such a strategy, Ottawa should review its position on China, and find a way to clearly articulate a stance that responds both to Beijing and the Indo-Pacific partners it is looking to cultivate. It can do this by avoiding hostility and clearly defining Canada’s national interests as well as its regional priorities. Then Ottawa can signal where compromise may be welcome, and where it is not. Positive engagement with Beijing, and freedom of navigation transits in the Taiwan Strait can both take place, but the government should articulate why both of those things matter.
